# Abstract

Reconstructing the long-run spatial demography of lowland and tropical South America requires reconciling prehistoric settlement archaeology, sixteenth-century riverine chronicles, colonial missionary and fiscal registers, and nineteenth- to twenty-first-century national censuses. Standard global historical databases such as the History Database of the Global Environment downscale continental and national estimates onto 5-arcminute raster grids through environmental suitability functions and distance-to-water proxies [@KleinGoldewijk2010; @KleinGoldewijk2011; @KleinGoldewijk2017]. For tropical South America, where human settlement transformed nutrient-poor oxisols into anthropogenic soils and established dense interfluvial settlements, top-down allocation models inevitably mischaracterise historical distributions. Foundational demographic syntheses, notably those of McEvedy and Jones (1978) and Maddison (2001), assigned conservative aggregate totals to Brazil and the tropical interior that reflected twentieth-century environmental determinism rather than archaeological evidence [@McEvedyJones1978; @Maddison2001]. PRETA provides a bottom-up demographic reconstruction spanning Amazonia, extra-Amazonian Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay and the Guianas across 12,65M km² from 10000BC to 2026AD.

PRETA synthesises fifteen constituent research monographs and coordinate-anchored settlement gazetteers, integrating 64.713 deduplicated archaeological site observations (compiled from over 110.000 raw entries across seventeen national and specialist registries after removing Brazilian CRM cluster duplicates within 1,2 km and Walker-Peripato earthwork overlaps within 1,5 km) alongside 1.323 explicit Amazonian Dark Earth anthrosol contexts across 1.272 sliver-merged HydroBASINS Level 6 hydrological catchments. The underlying corpus unites 21.484 deduplicated official site records from Brazil's Instituto do Patrimônio Histórico e Artístico Nacional [@IPHAN2024], 14.311 deduplicated pre-Hispanic monuments and 2.711 Qhapaq Ñan road and tambo nodes from Peru's Sistema de Información Geográfica de Arqueología [@SIGDA2024], 5.542 deduplicated sites from Colombia's Instituto Colombiano de Antropología e Historia [@ICANH2024], 4.693 South American radiocarbon determinations from PEOPLE 3000 p3k14c and AndesC14 [@Bird2022p3k14c; @Riris2018], 2.197 XRONOS radiocarbon dates for Bolivia and Peru incorporating the Bolivian Radiocarbon Database [@Capriles2023; @XRONOS2024], 419 OpenStreetMap and Wikidata Bolivian Highland archaeological localities, 316 systematic survey hubs from the PRETA Bolivian Highlands Gazetteer, 533 georeferenced Wikidata Andean monuments, 108 published Central Andean survey hubs [@Stanish2003; @Janusek2008; @Bauer2004], 2.080 morphologically classified Amazonian sites from Walker et al. [@Walker2023], 157 spatially unique remote-sensing earthworks from Peripato et al. [@Peripato2023], 2.778 radiocarbon-dated contexts from de Souza et al. [@deSouza2018], 56 transition records from Sales et al. [@Sales2021], 80 ring-ditch hill sites from French Guiana, 7.164 regional radiocarbon determinations and 84 canonical Terra Preta survey hubs. To model pre-Columbian settlement densities across terraced tropical Andean highlands, engineered Amazonian dark-earth bluffs and extra-Amazonian Brazil without sliver-polygon singularities or border discontinuities, PRETA solves a two-scale non-stationary Matérn covariance model ($\nu = 3/2$) with structural range parameters $\tau_1 = 1,50$ and $\tau_2 = 2,78$, evaluated across 1.039 active domestic catchments (99,90% coverage ratio) with a tropical Andean vertical-archipelago elevation profile, explicit C1 Terra Preta anthropogenic intensity coupling on pre-contact horizons (lifting Terra Preta corridors 3,73× to 6,15× above extra-Amazonian Eastern and Southern Brazil), dasymetric habitability tapering (leakage ratio 0,0001) and strong agreement with independent land-use models (logarithmic correlation 0,8693) [@PaciorekSchervish2006].

Across the pre-Columbian Holocene, population within the domain expanded from an initial forager baseline of 87,37k in 10000BC to 1,45M in 3000BC, 2,92M in 1000BC, 4,49M at 0AD and 9,57M at 1000AD. This expansion culminated in a late pre-Columbian apogee of 11,55M inhabitants in 1500AD across six hydrological domains: 6,24M in the Western Amazon Basin and Peruvian-Ecuadorian Andean Headwaters (3,65M in the Peruvian-Ecuadorian Andean Sierra and 2,59M across six lowland sub-basins) [@Cook1981; @DAltroy2015], 1,56M in Eastern Amazonia, 1,41M in the dedicated Bolivian Highlands module spanning Lake Titicaca, Tiwanaku, Chuquiabo-La Paz, Oruro, Cochabamba, Charcas and Potosí [@Stanish2003; @Janusek2008; @Capriles2023], 1,20M in Southern Brazil, 940k in North-Eastern Brazil and 204k in the Guianas. This pre-contact spatial hierarchy honours both the primacy of the Central Andes (with the Bolivian Highlands displaying 2,95× to 3,41× higher gridded density than the Bolivian Lowlands across 1000AD to 1500AD while preserving Llanos de Moxos as Bolivia's premier lowland urban hearth) and the superior agrarian carrying capacity of Amazonian Terra Preta river corridors relative to extra-Amazonian Brazil [@Heckenberger2003; @Prumers2022; @Rostain2024; @Schaan2008; @Clement2015; @Denevan1992].

Following initial European contact in 1500AD along the Brazilian Atlantic littoral, 1535AD in Upper Peru (Charcas), 1537AD in the Paraguay-Paraná basin, 1542AD along the Amazon mainstem and 1595AD on the Guiana coast, virgin-soil epidemics, colonial slaving and mining *mita* drafts triggered an acute demographic collapse, reducing indigenous populations by 70% to 90% across accessible corridors [@Hemming1978; @Sweet1974; @Newson1995; @Bakewell1984; @SanchezAlbornoz1978]. Aggregate population contracted sharply across the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries (Brazil bottoming at 1,97M in 1600AD, Colonial Upper Peru/Charcas dropping from 1,25M in 1535AD to 826k in 1700AD despite the Potosí silver boom, the Spanish Amazon missions at 467k in 1780AD and Paraguay at 158k in 1620AD). Demographic recovery began in the eighteenth century, propelled by transatlantic forced migration to sugar, tobacco and gold-mining economies and Andean agrarian rebound, followed by post-independence immigration, interior agricultural frontiers and late twentieth-century urbanisation. By 2026AD, the domain encompasses 232,1M residents, comprising Brazil (212,58M, ~213M) [@IBGE2023], Bolivia (11,53M) [@INE_Bolivia_2024], Paraguay (6,28M) [@INE_Paraguay_2022] and the Three Guianas (1,73M) [@BOS_Guyana_2016; @ABS_Suriname_2014; @INSEE_Guyane_2023].

# Background

Historical demographic reconstructions for tropical and lowland South America have long contended with the legacy of mid-twentieth-century environmental determinism. In her influential formulation of Amazonia as a counterfeit paradise, Betty Meggers argued that highly weathered tropical oxisols and ultisols imposed an immutable ecological ceiling on human cultural evolution, restricting pre-Columbian societies to small, semi-nomadic slash-and-burn villages incapable of sustaining permanent urbanism or dense sedentary populations [@Meggers1957]. Working within this paradigm, early global historical syntheses assigned minimalist numbers to lowland South America. Colin McEvedy and Richard Jones (1978) allocated exactly 1,0M inhabitants to the entirety of Brazil in 1500AD, with a further 750k apportioned across the remainder of the tropical lowlands, implying a continent virtually devoid of human modification before European arrival [@McEvedyJones1978]. Angus Maddison adopted similarly conservative figures in his millennial macroeconomic accounting, treating pre-Columbian South America outside the Andean cordillera as a negligible demographic quantity [@Maddison2001].

This minimalist orthodoxy was challenged by cultural geographers, historians and archaeologists who argued that pre-contact South American populations were substantially larger and geographically more extensive. William M. Denevan compiled ethnohistorical and ecological evidence demonstrating that pre-Columbian riverine densities were high and that greater Amazonia supported between 5,6M and 6,8M people on the eve of European contact [@Denevan1992]. Anna Roosevelt's stratigraphic excavations at the Caverna da Pedra Pintada in Pará established that Paleoindian foraging bands occupied the lower Amazon as early as 10000BC, producing some of the earliest ceramic traditions in the Western Hemisphere [@Roosevelt1996]. Subsequent archaeological research over the past three decades has overturned the notion of a pristine tropical wilderness. In the Upper Xingu basin, Michael Heckenberger and colleagues documented extensive networks of walled towns, circular plazas and 50-metre-wide arterial avenues linked to intensively managed agricultural parklands [@Heckenberger2003]. In the Llanos de Moxos of the southwestern Amazon, Umberto Lombardo and Heiko Prümers revealed that pre-Hispanic cultures constructed thousands of hectares of raised agricultural fields, canal systems and monumental platform mounds, culminating in low-density agrarian urbanism [@Lombardo2020; @Prumers2022]. Along the Upper Amazon and Upano valleys, Stéphen Rostain and co-authors identified vast ceremonial and residential earthwork complexes extending across hundreds of square kilometres [@Rostain2024].

A central pillar of this revised understanding is the discovery of Amazonian Dark Earths (Terra Preta de Índio and Terra Mulata). These anthropogenic anthrosols, created through centuries of organic waste accumulation, charcoal deposition and soil management, exhibit persistent fertility, high cation exchange capacity and elevated concentrations of phosphorus, calcium and magnesium [@Glaser2004; @Lehmann2003; @Woods2009]. Terra Preta sites occur along the mainstem floodplains of the Amazon and Tapajós, and likewise on well-drained tertiary bluffs and deep interfluvial plateaus, demonstrating that indigenous populations overcame tropical soil nutrient limitations to establish permanent agrarian settlements far beyond active riverbanks [@Clement2015; @McMichael2014; @Stenborg2012]. Recent remote-sensing and airborne LiDAR syntheses by Peripato et al. and de Souza et al. indicate that thousands of pre-Columbian earthwork structures remain concealed beneath the contemporary forest canopy, supporting model estimates of several million pre-Columbian inhabitants across the Amazon basin alone [@Peripato2023; @deSouza2018].

The environmental contrast between the fertile, annually inundated floodplains (várzea) and the nutrient-leached upland forests (terra firme) long formed the basis of ecological models in South American anthropology. While the várzea provided abundant aquatic protein and fertile alluvial silt, its narrow geographical extent—less than two percent of the Amazon basin—led early scholars to conclude that regional population capacity was severely constricted. However, archaeobotanical and pedological research has revealed that pre-Columbian populations transformed terra firme soils into durable agricultural landscapes through the deliberate synthesis of biochar, domestic refuse and bone meal, creating extensive Terra Mulata agricultural fields alongside residential Terra Preta deposits [@Glaser2004; @Woods2009; @Clement2015]. Furthermore, indigenous management of economic tree species—such as the peach palm (*Bactris gasipaes*), Brazil nut (*Bertholletia excelsa*), cacao (*Theobroma cacao*) and açai (*Euterpe oleracea*)—enriched the forest canopy, creating domesticated cultural forests with carrying capacities far exceeding unmanaged climax vegetation [@Clement2015; @Lombardo2020].

Early European chronicles provide vivid qualitative corroboration of dense riverine populations. The Dominican friar Gaspar de Carvajal, recording Francisco de Orellana's historic 1541-1542AD descent of the Amazon, described continuous riverbank settlements stretching across dozens of leagues in the territory of the Omagua and Machiparo confederacies [@Sweet1974; @Hemming1978]. Carvajal noted palisaded towns, multi-roomed communal dwellings, fleets of war canoes carrying hundreds of warriors, and extensive agricultural storehouses filled with dried fish, roasted manioc flour and fermented beverages. A century later, in 1639AD, the Jesuit chronicler Cristóbal de Acuña accompanied Pedro Teixeira's upriver navigation, observing that the river islands and bluffs remained populated, though European epidemic diseases had already begun their devastating progression. Along the Atlantic coast of Brazil, early Portuguese and French observers, including Pero Vaz de Caminha in 1500AD, Hans Staden in 1557AD and Jean de Léry in 1578AD, recorded populous Tupinambá villages organised in communal malocas, capable of mobilising regional confederacies of several thousand warriors.

When the History Database of the Global Environment (HYDE 3.1 and HYDE 3.2) introduced gridded historical population maps at 5-arcminute resolution, it represented a major methodological advance by distributing historical numbers using physical geography proxies, including coastlines, navigable rivers, slopes and climate [@KleinGoldewijk2010; @KleinGoldewijk2011; @KleinGoldewijk2017]. However, global models inherently rely on national-level control totals and universal suitability weighting. In tropical South America, where historical population distribution was governed by regional soil anthrosol creation, raised-field construction and specialised riverine versus interfluvial subsistence strategies, global weighting surfaces concentrate population along modern urban corridors or narrow floodplain strips while underallocating settlement to historically documented earthwork and dark-earth complexes. Furthermore, global gridded series struggle to capture the asynchronous timing of the post-1500AD demographic collapse across distinct river basins and colonial frontiers.

Historical evidence for South American population is stratified across five distinct documentary and physical records:

1. Prehistoric archaeology and archaeobotany, consisting of 64.713 deduplicated site observations (compiled from over 110.000 raw records across Brazilian IPHAN SICG, Peruvian Ministry of Culture SIGDA, Colombian ICANH, PEOPLE 3000 p3k14c/AndesC14, XRONOS Capriles Bolivian Radiocarbon Database, Bolivian Highlands systematic surveys and Amazonian earthwork inventories), 1.323 catalogued Terra Preta occurrences, coastal shell mounds (sambaquis), geometric geoglyphs, Andean terraced cities and radiocarbon chronologies extending from the terminal Pleistocene to the contact horizon [@IPHAN2024; @SIGDA2024; @ICANH2024; @Bird2022p3k14c; @Capriles2023; @XRONOS2024].
2. Contact-period chronicles and voyage logs, including the sixteenth- and seventeenth-century accounts of Francisco de Orellana (1542AD), Cristóbal de Acuña (1639AD), Hans Staden (1557AD), Jean de Léry (1578AD) and Ulrich Schmidl (1567AD), which document continuous riverine settlements and large chiefdoms before the full devastation of European epidemics.
3. Colonial ecclesiastical, fiscal and administrative documentation, spanning the annual letters (*cartas anuas*) and reduction censuses of the Society of Jesus in Paraguay and Moxos, parish registers of baptisms and burials, captaincy hearth books (*fogos*) and late eighteenth-century governor tallies conducted under the Pombaline and Bourbon administrative reforms [@Marcilio1984; @Alden1963; @Maeder1980; @Schwartz1985].
4. Nineteenth-century post-independence national counts, including the landmark 1872 General Census of the Empire of Brazil [@IBGE1874], early republican enumerations in Bolivia and Paraguay, and documentation of catastrophic wartime mortality, notably the War of the Triple Alliance (1864-1870AD) which eliminated over half of Paraguay's population [@WhighamPotthast1999; @Maeder1984].
5. Modern national statistical census systems, administered by the Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística in Brazil, the Instituto Nacional de Estadística in Bolivia and Paraguay, the Institut National de la Statistique et des Études Économiques in French Guiana, the Algemeen Bureau voor de Statistiek in Suriname and the Bureau of Statistics in Guyana [@IBGE2023; @INE_Bolivia_2024; @INE_Paraguay_2022; @INSEE_Guyane_2023; @ABS_Suriname_2014; @BOS_Guyana_2016].

PRETA harmonises these five evidentiary traditions into an integrated spatial-demographic framework. By linking multi-repository archaeological datasets to non-stationary Matérn kriging surfaces and historical settlement gazetteers, PRETA reconstructs long-run demographic trajectories across 12,65M km² from 10000BC to 2026AD without artificial administrative seams or ahistorical backward projections.

# Architecture of the Fifteen Regional Studies

To capture shifting geopolitical boundaries, distinct ecological zones and divergent colonial administrative trajectories without territorial gaps across the Bolivian Altiplano or Eastern Cordillera, PRETA partitions its spatial domain into fifteen constituent research monographs organised across three chronological regimes (Table 1 and Figure 1).

## Regime 1: Pre-Columbian Regional Polities (10000BC to 1595AD)

The first regime comprises six pre-Columbian regional studies spanning the Holocene from 10000BC to European contact (1500AD in coastal Brazil, 1535AD in the Bolivian Highlands, 1542AD in the Amazon mainstem and 1595AD in the Guianas). The South American continent north of the Río de la Plata forms three interconnected fluvial macro-basins alongside the endorheic Titicaca-Poopó Altiplano: the Amazon, the Orinoco-Guiana littoral, the Paraná-Paraguay system and the Central Andean highlands. During the pre-Columbian Holocene, human migration, camelid caravan exchange and fluvial trade flowed across these systems, creating cultural horizons linked by terraced agriculture, polychrome ceramics, raised-field engineering and dark-earth soil technology.

### Eastern Amazon Basin (10000BC to 1542AD)

The Eastern Amazon Basin module (2.685.138 km²) encompasses Marajó Island, the lower Amazon mainstem, the Tapajós confluence at Santarém, the Xinguano headwaters and the Tocantins-Araguaia basin [@Schaan2008; @Nimuendaju1952; @Stenborg2012]. The region contains major pre-Columbian ceramic traditions, from the early pottery of the Mina phase to the elaborate polychrome urns of the Marajoara mounds and the modelled iconography of Santarém. At its pre-contact peak in 1500AD, the Eastern Amazon supported 1,56M inhabitants, sustained by intensive riverine fisheries, floodplain agriculture and extensive Terra Preta settlements on high bluffs. The Upper Xingu sub-region hosted interconnected networks of circular plaza villages integrated by wide straight roads and defensive moats, housing an engineered agricultural population of 30k to 50k people [@Heckenberger2003].

Prehistoric occupation in the Eastern Amazon was anchored by early ceramic complexes at Pedra Pintada and the Taperinha shell mound near Santarém, dating to 6000BC-4000BC. By 500AD, the Marajoara culture transformed the seasonally inundated savannas of eastern Marajó Island through the construction of earthen mounds up to twelve metres high, functioning as residential platforms for elite lineages, ceremonial feasting centres and cemetery complexes [@Schaan2008; @Meggers1957]. Farther upriver, the Tapajó chiefdom established an expansive polity centred at the mouth of the Tapajós, where anthrosol deposits exceed one hundred hectares, indicating a high-density nucleated settlement capable of sustaining specialised craft production and hierarchical governance [@Nimuendaju1952; @Stenborg2012]. In the Tocantins-Araguaia basin, extensive circular ring villages and rock-art complexes marked trade corridors linking the eastern forest to the central Brazilian plateau.

The spatial distribution of Terra Preta anthrosols along the lower Amazon and Tapajós bluffs points to sustained sedentism rather than ephemeral shifting cultivation. At sites such as Belterra, Santarém-Aldeia and Juruti, dark-earth horizons reach depths of over two metres, enriched with pottery sherds, aquatic bone residues and pyrogenic carbon [@Stenborg2012; @Glaser2004; @Woods2009]. These bluff-top settlements commanded expansive views of the várzea floodplains, providing immediate access to seasonal aquatic protein while avoiding annual flood pulses. Ethnohistorical accounts by Carvajal and later chroniclers describe continuous riverside settlements stretching for leagues, corroborating the archaeological evidence of dense agrarian settlements supported by intensive root-crop agroforestry and riverine fisheries.

### Western Amazon Basin and Peruvian-Ecuadorian Andean Headwaters (10000BC to 1542AD)

The Western Amazon Basin and Peruvian-Ecuadorian Andean Headwaters module (4.186.006 km²) spans the western Amazonian watershed from the Negro-Solimões confluence westward to the Pacific continental divide of Peru and Ecuador, partitioned into seven organic HydroBASINS divisions [@Neves2022; @Prumers2022; @Lombardo2020; @Cook1981; @Bauer2004]. Combining the imperial agrarian heartlands of the Peruvian-Ecuadorian Andean Sierra (3,65M in 1500AD across Cusco, Wari, Mantaro, Huánuco, Chavín, Cajamarca, Chachapoyas and Tomebamba) with six lowland Amazonian divisions (2,59M in 1500AD across Central Amazonia, Madeira-Guaporé, Llanos de Moxos, Acre-Purus, Solimões-Caquetá and Lower Marañón-Ucayali), the watershed reached 6,24M inhabitants in 1500AD before contracting to 5,33M by 1542AD under early pandemic and conquest shocks [@Cook1981; @DAltroy2015; @SIGDA2024].

In the southwestern Amazon, across Acre and northern Rondônia, archaeological surveys have documented more than 900 geometric ditched enclosures (geoglyphs) constructed between 1000BC and 1000AD, exhibiting sophisticated spatial geometry and regional connectivity [@Peripato2023; @deSouza2018]. In the Upper Amazon and Upano River valleys of modern Ecuador, recent airborne LiDAR surveys revealed extensive garden urbanism consisting of thousands of residential mounds, ceremonial complexes and agricultural terraces interconnected by sunken roads dating from 500BC to 600AD [@Rostain2024]. Along the Madeira and Guaporé river corridors, dense ceramic traditions flourished, functioning as primary linguistic and cultural conduits between the Amazonian lowlands and the Chaco-Plata systems.

In the seasonally inundated savannas of the Llanos de Moxos, indigenous engineering achieved monumental scale through hydrological management [@Lombardo2020; @Prumers2022]. Communities excavated thousands of linear canals and constructed raised agricultural platforms covering tens of thousands of hectares, draining excess floodwaters during the wet season while retaining moisture during dry months. Interconnecting these agricultural zones were elevated earthen causeways (*terraplenes*) that stretched across the landscape for kilometres, linking habitable forest islands (*islas de bosque*) and ceremonial mound centres. Radiometric dating indicates that hydraulic landscape modification began as early as 1000BC and reached its demographic zenith between 500AD and 1400AD under the Casarabe culture, representing one of the earliest cases of agrarian urbanism in the tropical Americas.

### North-Eastern Brazil (10000BC to 1500AD)

The North-Eastern Brazil module (1.881.594 km²) encompasses the semi-arid Caatinga, the Serra da Capivara rock-art sanctuaries, the perennial corridor of the São Francisco River and the Atlantic forest littoral occupied by Tupinambá horticultural polities. Pre-Columbian settlement in the interior depended on strategic access to perennial springs and granite inselbergs, while the humid coastal strip supported dense semi-sedentary villages subsisting on bitter manioc cultivation, shellfish collection and coastal fishing, reaching 940k inhabitants in 1500AD.

Archaeological investigations in the Serra da Capivara National Park in Piauí have documented over 1.300 prehistoric sites, featuring thousands of painted panels depicting anthropomorphic ceremonies, hunting scenes and megafaunal encounters belonging to the Nordeste and Agreste rock-art traditions. In the late Holocene, agrarian groups producing Itaparica and Aratu-Sapucaí ceramics occupied the fertile alluvial floodplains of the São Francisco River, establishing permanent settlements that served as trade corridors between the interior savannas and the Atlantic forest coast. Along the restinga sand dunes and mangrove estuaries of the Atlantic littoral, populous Tupinambá villages maintained continuous coastal territories, managing estuarine fisheries alongside manioc plantations.

During the mid-Holocene arid phase between 6000BC and 3000BC, environmental drying forced hunter-gatherer groups in the semi-arid interior to concentrate around resilient micro-climatic refuges, such as the humid highland enclaves (*brejos de altitude*) and perennial spring lines of the Chapada Diamantina and Serra da Capivara. With the return of wetter conditions in the late Holocene, agrarian populations producing pottery of the Aratu tradition expanded across the sertão and into the São Francisco valley, establishing ring-shaped villages with central mortuary plazas. These interior horticulturalists cultivated maize, beans and manioc along seasonal riverbanks, maintaining regular exchange networks with coastal Tupinambá polities that supplied marine shells, salt and feather ornaments.

### Southern Brazil (10000BC to 1500AD)

The Southern Brazil module (1.920.483 km²) covers the Atlantic coastal sambaqui shell mounds, the highland Araucaria plateau dominated by Southern Jê pit-house settlements, the upper Paraná and Uruguay river basins settled by Guarani agriculturalists and the southern Pampa wetland mounds (cerritos). Coastal sambaquis reached their apogee between 3000BC and 1000BC, while the late Holocene was characterised by the demographic expansion of Guarani and Jê groups, sustaining 1,20M people in 1500AD.

The coastal sambaquis of Santa Catarina and Rio de Janeiro represent some of the most massive hunter-gatherer monuments in the world, with shell and sediment mounds reaching thirty metres in height and containing hundreds of intentional human interments, indicating stable, territorial populations with maritime economies. In the interior highlands of Paraná, Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul, Southern Jê populations adapted to the Araucaria moist forests, constructing semi-subterranean pit-house villages and ceremonial dance enclosures (*dançadores*) associated with the intensive exploitation of pine nuts (*Araucaria angustifolia*). Simultaneously, Guarani horticulturalists expanded along the major river corridors, introducing polychrome ceramics and shifting maize-manioc agriculture. In the southern wetlands of Rio Grande do Sul, indigenous groups constructed earthen mounds (*cerritos de indios*) to secure elevated ground for settlements, burials and garden cultivation in seasonally flooded grasslands.

In the elevated plateau forests of southern Brazil, the Taquara-Itararé ceramic tradition, associated with ancestral Southern Jê populations, engineered subterranean settlements adapted to montane frost regimes. Excavations have uncovered semi-subterranean pit houses ranging from two to twenty metres in diameter and up to seven metres in depth, clustered in nucleated villages containing communal food-storage structures and central ceremonial mounds. These highland settlements relied on the seasonal gathering and storage of Araucaria pine nuts (*pinhão*), combined with hunting of forest game and small-scale horticulture. Radiocarbon sequences demonstrate sustained demographic expansion between 800AD and 1400AD, culminating in the construction of monumental earthwork enclosures that functioned as regional mortuary and political centres.

### Pre-Columbian Guianas (10000BC to 1595AD)

The Pre-Columbian Guianas module (453.868 km²) encompasses the coastal mangrove littoral, raised agricultural ridges, interior savannas and ditch-enclosed hill settlements (Montagnes Couronnées) across modern Guyana, Suriname and French Guiana [@Rostain2008]. Coastal indigenous communities engineered extensive drainage canals and agricultural mounds to cultivate manioc in seasonally inundated wetlands, sustaining 204k inhabitants in 1500AD.

The archaeological sequence of the Guianas reflects sophisticated landscape adaptations. Along the coast, Archaic populations established pre-ceramic shell mounds from 4000BC onward, succeeded by Barrancoid and Arauquinoid ceramic complexes associated with raised agricultural fields. In the coastal savannas of Suriname and French Guiana, indigenous farmers constructed grids of elevated agricultural mounds that prevented root waterlogging while concentrating organic nutrients [@Rostain2008]. In the forested hills of French Guiana, communities built fortified ring-ditch structures atop strategic hilltops, providing defensive refuges and ritual spaces. Across the interior savannas of the Rupununi and Sipaliwini, petroglyph panels and polished stone implements document ancient overland trade routes linking the Caribbean littoral to the Amazon mainstem.

Along the dynamic coastline of Suriname and French Guiana, Arauquinoid farming communities adapted to coastal marine inundation through extensive raised-field architecture [@Rostain2008]. Between 650AD and 1400AD, indigenous populations transformed flooded coastal savannas into patterned grids of circular and rectangular agricultural mounds, elevated thirty to one hundred centimetres above high water levels. These raised beds prevented root suffocation while concentrating organic matter and aerating soil profiles, generating agricultural yields sufficient to support dense, nucleated settlements. Similar earthworks have been recorded in the coastal wetlands of Guyana, demonstrating a coordinated technological response across the entire Guiana littoral to the challenges of coastal mangrove farming.

### Pre-Columbian Bolivian Highlands (10000BC to 1535AD)

The Pre-Columbian Bolivian Highlands module (405.375 km²) spans the entire endorheic Titicaca-Desaguadero-Poopó Altiplano and the adjoining Eastern Cordillera inter-Andean valleys of La Paz, Cochabamba, Chuquisaca, Potosí and Tarija across six organic HydroBASINS Level 6 basins [@Stanish2003; @Janusek2008; @Capriles2023]. Anchored by 316 georeferenced pre-Hispanic settlements verified from XRONOS Capriles radiocarbon series, OpenStreetMap, Wikidata and regional valley surveys, highland Bolivia evolved from early Archaic *viscachani* foraging bands (7,05k in 10000BC) through Formative Chiripa and Wankarani villages (304,2k in 1000BC) to the monumental Middle Horizon Tiwanaku urban state centred on the Koani Pampa raised fields (1,22M in 1000AD, with Tiwanaku reaching 35k and Lukurmata 11k). Following Tiwanaku's eleventh-century decentralisation into fortified Aymara *señoríos* (*pucaras*), Inca *Qullasuyu* incorporation expanded imperial granary estates in Cochabamba (2.400 *qollqas* at Cotapachi) and frontier fortresses such as Incallajta, lifting highland population to 1,41M by 1500AD (347,8 persons per 100 km² — an order of magnitude above the adjacent Amazonian lowlands) before contracting to 1,25M by 1535AD.

## Regime 2: Colonial Administration and Frontiers (1500AD to 1825AD)

The second regime encompasses five colonial modules that track administrative, mining and missionary reorganisations between 1500AD and national independence (1811-1825AD). While the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494AD) theoretically restricted Portuguese settlement to eastern Brazil, Portuguese bandeirantes, Jesuit missionaries and military expeditions progressively expanded Portuguese sovereignty westward across the Amazon and south-westward into Mato Grosso and Rio Grande do Sul. Concurrently, Spanish imperial power consolidated around the silver mines of Upper Peru (Real Audiencia de Charcas) and its surrounding missionary provinces, before the 1750AD Treaty of Madrid formally ratified Iberian frontiers across the continent.

### Colonial Brazil (1500AD to 1822AD)

Colonial Brazil (8.544.864 km²) covers the hereditary captaincies, the coastal sugar engenhos of Bahia and Pernambuco reliant on transatlantic African slave labour, the interior slaving and prospecting routes (*bandeiras*), the eighteenth-century gold and diamond boom in Minas Gerais and the northern State of Grão-Pará and Maranhão [@Marcilio1984; @Alden1963; @Schwartz1985; @Klein2010; @Hemming1978]. Colonial demographic dynamics were driven by catastrophic indigenous depopulation, massive slave importation and interior mining migrations, bottoming at 1,97M in 1600AD before rebounding to 4,54M by 1822AD.

The institutional framework of colonial Brazil was established through fifteen hereditary captaincies granted by the Portuguese Crown in the 1530s, followed by the appointment of a Governor-General at Salvador da Bahia in 1549AD. The rapid expansion of sugar mills (*engenhos*) along the Recôncavo of Bahia and the coastal plains of Pernambuco generated a commercial monoculture requiring substantial forced labour. The eighteenth-century gold and diamond discoveries in Minas Gerais, Goiás and Mato Grosso triggered a major interior migration that drew hundreds of thousands of free and enslaved people into the central highlands, culminating in the transfer of the colonial viceregal capital to Rio de Janeiro in 1763AD [@Alden1963; @Schwartz1985].

Throughout the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, the demographic foundation of Portuguese Brazil rested upon a contested frontier between coastal plantations and interior indigenous societies. The initial reliance on enslaved indigenous labour in the sugar fields of Bahia and Pernambuco collapsed under the combined weight of epidemic contagion, armed resistance and Jesuit opposition, prompting colonial authorities to enact legislation restricting indigenous bondage while increasing the importation of enslaved Africans [@Marcilio1984; @Schwartz1985]. Simultaneously, Paulista *bandeiras* mounted deep slaving expeditions into the interior, devastating Jesuit missions in Guairá and the upper Paraná basin and capturing tens of thousands of indigenous captives. The subsequent eighteenth-century mining boom shifted the demographic centre of gravity southward toward Minas Gerais, fostering rapid urban growth in towns like Ouro Preto, Mariana and Diamantina.

### Colonial Guianas (1595AD to 1815AD)

Colonial Guianas (453.932 km²) traces Dutch, British and French plantation settlements along the Essequibo, Demerara, Berbice, Suriname and Cayenne river estuaries, alongside autonomous Maroon societies that formed in the forested interior [@Oostindie2005]. Coastal poldering required immense labour inputs, creating plantation societies dominated by enslaved Africans that reached 224k in 1815AD.

The colonial history of the Guianas was shaped by continuous geopolitical conflict among European powers. The Dutch West India Company established permanent trading posts along the Essequibo in 1616AD and developed extensive sugar, coffee and cotton plantations protected by dykes and sluices. In Suriname, the harsh conditions of chattel slavery stimulated repeated escapes into the interior rainforests, where Maroons established autonomous military polities; the Dutch colonial administration was eventually forced to negotiate formal peace treaties with the Ndyuka in 1760AD and the Saramaka in 1762AD, formally recognising their territorial autonomy [@Oostindie2005].

### Colonial Paraguay (1537AD to 1811AD)

Colonial Paraguay (415.304 km²) examines the Asunción governorate, the encomienda system, the thirty Jesuit Guaraní missions established between 1609AD and their 1767AD expulsion, and the turbulent Gran Chaco frontier [@Maeder1980; @Alden1996]. The Jesuit reductions established self-contained agrarian communities with communal storehouses, cattle ranches and craft workshops, shielding indigenous populations from bandeirante raids and maintaining 193k inhabitants in 1811AD.

Founded in 1537AD as the administrative centre of the Río de la Plata, Asunción served as the base for the settlement of Buenos Aires, Santa Cruz de la Sierra and Corrientes. Due to its geographic isolation and absence of precious metals, colonial Paraguay developed a subsistence economy based on the encomienda of Guaraní villagers, cattle pastoralism and yerba mate harvesting. The thirty Jesuit missions represented a remarkable socio-demographic institution, maintaining complete parish registers of baptisms, marriages and burials, and sustaining an aggregate population of more than 100k until the 1767AD royal decree expelled the order from the Spanish Empire [@Maeder1980].

### Colonial Spanish Amazon (1542AD to 1825AD)

The Colonial Spanish Amazon module (1.874.185 km²) covers the missionary and administrative frontiers of the Comandancia General de Maynas, the Gobernación de Quijos-Canelos-Macas, the Franciscan and Capuchin stations along the Caquetá and Putumayo, and the Jesuit missions of Moxos and Chiquitos [@Block1994; @Newson1995; @Sweet1974; @Radding2005]. Frontier missions suffered persistent epidemic waves and indigenous uprisings, falling from 1,325M in 1542AD to a nadir of 467k in 1780AD before recovering modestly to 506k by 1825AD.

The Spanish colonial presence in the Amazonian lowlands was conducted by religious orders operating from Andean bases in Quito, Lima and Santa Fe de Bogotá. The Jesuit Province of Maynas, founded in 1638AD, established missions among the Maina, Omagua, Cocama and Jebero along the Marañón, Huallaga and Ucayali rivers, but mission populations were repeatedly decimated by measles and smallpox epidemics [@Block1994; @Newson1995]. In lowland Bolivia, the Jesuit missions of Moxos and Chiquitos developed thriving cattle and agricultural economies that survived under secular clergy after 1767AD, maintaining distinct indigenous town councils.

In the southwestern Amazon, the Jesuit missions of Moxos and Chiquitos established an autonomous demographic and socio-economic regime distinct from the Andean highlands [@Block1994; @Radding2005]. From 1682AD until 1767AD, Jesuit missionaries congregated over thirty thousand Moxeño and Chiquitano neophytes into compact mission towns (*reducciones*). Unlike the demographic devastation that afflicted encomienda zones in the Andean valleys, the Moxos and Chiquitos missions maintained demographic stability through diversified pastoral economies, communal cattle ranches, irrigated horticulture and baroque musical and artisanal production. Following the expulsion of the Jesuits in 1767AD, civil administrators took control of the missions, which led to administrative disruption, labour exploitation and partial dispersal of mission populations into surrounding forest refuges.

### Colonial Bolivian Highlands — Real Audiencia de Charcas (1535AD to 1825AD)

The Colonial Bolivian Highlands module (468.807 km²) covers the six core highland and valley jurisdictions of the Real Audiencia de Charcas (Intendencias of La Paz, Oruro, Cochabamba, Charcas/Chuquisaca, Potosí and Tarija), splicing directly from Pre-Columbian Bolivian Highlands in 1535AD (1,25M) to Bolivia after Independence in 1825AD (998k across the six highland departments) with zero spatial overlap or temporal discontinuity [@Bakewell1984; @Tandeter1993; @SanchezAlbornoz1978; @Larson1998; @Klein2011]. Anchored by 258 catalogued *reducción* towns, mining villas and parish seats, the region experienced the hemisphere's largest urban mining boom after the 1545AD Cerro Rico silver discovery at Potosí (peaking at 160k residents around 1610AD under Viceroy Toledo's *mita* labour draft and mercury amalgamation), alongside Oruro (48k), La Paz (38k), Cochabamba (30,5k) and Chuquisaca-Sucre (19,8k). Prolonged epidemic mortality, *mita* out-migration of *forasteros* into Cochabamba and La Paz valleys and seventeenth-century silver exhaustion depressed regional population to 826k by 1700AD, before agrarian recovery and Bourbon-era trade lifted Upper Peru to 998k at independence in 1825AD.

## Regime 3: Post-Independence Modern Expansion (1811AD to 2026AD)

The third regime comprises four post-independence modules extending to 2026AD. The collapse of Iberian imperial authority between 1811AD and 1825AD created independent nation-states that inherited vast, sparsely populated frontier territories. Throughout the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, state-led colonisation programmes, railway and highway construction, and international migration transformed lowland South America from an extractive frontier into one of the world's most dynamic agrarian and urban macro-regions.

### Brazil after Independence (1822AD to 2026AD)

Brazil after Independence (8.545.413 km²) traces the transition from the Empire of Brazil (1822-1889AD) to the First Republic, the expansion of the São Paulo coffee frontier, mass European and East Asian immigration, Vargas-era industrialisation, the construction of Brasília, the westward expansion of modern agro-industrial frontiers and contemporary IBGE municipal censuses [@IBGE1874; @IBGE2023]. National population increased from 4,25M in 1822AD to 10,00M in 1872, 41,24M in 1940 and 212,58M (~213M) by 2026AD.

Following independence in 1822AD, the Empire of Brazil maintained political stability under Pedro I and Pedro II, conducting the first general census of the empire in 1872AD, which enumerated 9.930.478 free inhabitants and 1.510.806 enslaved persons [@IBGE1874]. The abolition of slavery in 1888AD coincided with the massive expansion of coffee plantations in the Paraíba Valley and western São Paulo, stimulating state-subsidised immigration from Italy, Portugal, Spain, Germany and Japan. In the mid-twentieth century, state-led industrialisation under Getúlio Vargas and Juscelino Kubitschek accelerated rural-to-urban migration, culminating in the inauguration of Brasília in 1960AD and the rapid urbanisation of the Southeast and South [@IBGE2023].

The late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries witnessed the integration of the Amazon basin into global industrial trade through the rubber boom (1879-1912AD). The international demand for wild Amazonian latex (*Hevea brasiliensis*) drew hundreds of thousands of migrant workers, primarily subsistence farmers fleeing severe droughts in the north-eastern state of Ceará, into the western Amazon river valleys of Acre, Amazonas and Pará. This internal migration led to the founding of riverine trading posts, transformed Belém and Manaus into rubber metropolises with European architecture, and triggered border disputes that resulted in the 1903AD Treaty of Petrópolis, incorporating Acre into Brazilian territory. Following the collapse of the Amazonian rubber boom due to Southeast Asian plantation competition, the demographic trajectory of Brazil shifted decisively toward the industrialising Southeast, while the mid-twentieth century witnessed the construction of Belém-Brasília highway corridors and the agro-industrial settlement of the central-western Cerrado [@IBGE2023].

### Bolivia after Independence (1825AD to 2026AD)

Bolivia after Independence (1.115.871 km²) examines nineteenth-century demographic stagnation in the Andean Altiplano, the late nineteenth-century Amazonian rubber boom in the Beni and Acre corridors, the post-1952 agrarian revolution and the modern eastward demographic shift toward Santa Cruz de la Sierra [@INE_Bolivia_2024]. Population expanded from 1,18M in 1825AD to 11,53M in 2026AD.

Throughout the nineteenth century, Bolivia's demographic centre remained anchored in the Andean Altiplano and inter-Andean valleys around La Paz, Cochabamba, Sucre and Potosí. The late nineteenth-century rubber boom triggered an influx of extractors and indigenous forced labourers into the Amazonian departments of Beni and Pando, culminating in the Acre War (1899-1903AD) and the cession of Acre to Brazil. Following the 1952 National Revolution, state investment in road infrastructure and agricultural settlement catalyzed the growth of Santa Cruz de la Sierra, which evolved from a peripheral outpost into the nation's economic powerhouse, housing over 2,5M residents in its metropolitan area by 2026AD [@INE_Bolivia_2024].

### Paraguay after Independence (1811AD to 2026AD)

Paraguay after Independence (415.304 km²) analyses the insular state capitalism of José Gaspar Rodríguez de Francia, the demographic devastation of the War of the Triple Alliance, post-war recovery, the Chaco War (1932-1935AD) and twentieth-century agricultural colonisation [@WhighamPotthast1999; @Whigham2002; @Maeder1984; @INE_Paraguay_2022]. Population contracted from 489k in 1864AD to 221k in 1870AD before recovering to 6,28M in 2026AD.

Under the authoritarian rule of Dr. Francia (1814-1840AD) and Carlos Antonio López (1844-1862AD), Paraguay developed a state-directed economy with high social stability and self-sufficiency. However, the disastrous War of the Triple Alliance (1864-1870AD) under Francisco Solano López resulted in the death of over half the national population through combat, starvation and disease [@WhighamPotthast1999; @Whigham2002]. In the twentieth century, Paraguay successfully defended its western territory in the Chaco War (1932-1935AD), encouraged Mennonite agricultural colonisation in the arid Chaco, and experienced rapid agrarian expansion in the eastern borderlands during the construction of the Itaipu hydroelectric dam in the 1970s [@INE_Paraguay_2022].

### Guianas post-1815 (1815AD to 2026AD)

Guianas post-1815 (453.932 km²) documents the abolition of slavery across British Guiana (1834AD), French Guiana (1848AD) and Dutch Suriname (1863AD), subsequent indentured labour migration from India, Indonesia and China, post-colonial political transitions and contemporary offshore energy developments [@BOS_Guyana_2016; @ABS_Suriname_2014; @INSEE_Guyane_2023]. The region grew from 230,9k in 1815AD to 1,73M in 2026AD.

The abolition of slavery transformed the Guianas into plural societies through the recruitment of indentured workers to replace emancipated plantation labourers. British Guiana received over 238k Indian and 13k Chinese immigrants; Suriname imported 34k Indian and 33k Javanese workers; French Guiana remained sparsely populated, serving as a penal colony until 1953AD [@Oostindie2005]. Post-colonial transitions saw Guyana achieve independence in 1966AD and Suriname in 1975AD, while French Guiana was integrated as an overseas department of France. In the twenty-first century, major offshore oil discoveries off the Guyanese coast have made Guyana one of the world's fastest-growing economies, transforming demographic and urban dynamics across the Guiana Shield [@BOS_Guyana_2016].

Following the mid-nineteenth-century abolition of slavery across the British, French and Dutch colonies, the settlement geography of the Guianas diverged into distinct spatial patterns [@Oostindie2005]. Emancipated Afro-descendant populations pooled financial resources to purchase abandoned sugar plantations collectively, establishing autonomous communal villages along the coastal road network. Concurrently, colonial plantation owners recruited indentured agricultural labourers from British India, the Netherlands East Indies (Java) and southern China under indentured labour contracts. In British Guiana and Suriname, these Asian immigrant communities settled predominantly in estate barracks and peripheral agricultural polders, cultivating wet rice and market vegetables. This demographic restructuring established the dual ethnic and spatial character of modern Guyana and Suriname, contrasting with French Guiana, which remained demographically constrained by its role as a penal colony centred on Devil's Island and Saint-Laurent-du-Maroni until the mid-twentieth century [@BOS_Guyana_2016; @ABS_Suriname_2014; @INSEE_Guyane_2023].

# Multi-Repository Archaeology and Terra Preta Anthrosol Kriging

To reconstruct pre-Columbian population densities across the Central Andean highlands, the Bolivian Altiplano, the Amazonian dark-earth corridors and extra-Amazonian Brazil without relying on modern settlement distributions, PRETA establishes a multi-repository archaeological database harmonising seventeen primary registers spanning Brazil, Peru, Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador, Paraguay and the Three Guianas (Table 2).

The eastern lowland and Atlantic baseline is anchored by Brazil's Instituto do Patrimônio Histórico e Artístico Nacional through the Sistema Integrado de Conhecimento e Gestão (21.484 spatially deduplicated pre-Columbian sites from 32.933 raw records after removing 1,2 km CRM survey cluster duplicates) [@IPHAN2024], alongside Walker et al. (2.080 Amazonian ADE and earthwork sites) [@Walker2023], Peripato et al. (157 spatially unique remote-sensing earthworks after removing 804 duplicates overlapping Walker within 1,5 km) [@Peripato2023], de Souza et al. (2.778 radiocarbon contexts) [@deSouza2018], Sales et al. (56 transition records) [@Sales2021], DOPAMICS French Guiana (80 ring-ditch and ADE pits), the SVEA continental radiocarbon corpus (7.164 dates) and the Canonical Terra Preta Literature Atlas (84 hubs) [@Glaser2004; @Lehmann2003; @Woods2009]. To eliminate historical survey imbalance across both the Peruvian Sierra and the Bolivian Highlands, PRETA incorporates Peru's official SIGDA national monument cadastre (14.311 deduplicated pre-Hispanic monuments plus 2.711 Qhapaq Ñan road and tambo nodes) [@SIGDA2024], Colombia's official ICANH registry (5.542 deduplicated sites from 22.146 raw records) [@ICANH2024], PEOPLE 3000 p3k14c and AndesC14 radiocarbon determinations (4.693 dates) [@Bird2022p3k14c; @Riris2018], 2.197 XRONOS radiocarbon dates for Bolivia and Peru incorporating the Bolivian Radiocarbon Database [@Capriles2023; @XRONOS2024], 419 OpenStreetMap and Wikidata Bolivian Highland sites, 316 georeferenced hubs from the PRETA Bolivian Highlands Survey Gazetteer, 533 Wikidata Andean monuments and 108 published Central Andean survey hubs [@Stanish2003; @Janusek2008; @Bauer2004; @Cook1981].

In total, PRETA compiles 64.713 deduplicated composite archaeological records (over 110.000 raw primary entries), including 1.323 explicit Amazonian Dark Earth (Terra Preta de Índio) locations. Folding 363 sub-2.200 km² HydroBASINS river-confluence sliver polygons into nearest same-biome catchments eliminates artificial low-area areal-density singularities in lowland Bolivia (such as Riberalta), while three-tier macro-biome taphonomic outlier conditioning (Andes, Amazonia-Terra Preta and Extra-Amazonian Brazil) preserves an empirical 5,68× higher areal archaeological intensity in the Bolivian Highlands relative to the Bolivian Lowlands at 1500AD (27,75 vs. 4,88 weighted sites per 1.000 km²). Coupled with a dedicated tropical Andean vertical-archipelago elevation profile (honouring Quechua maize valleys at 2.400–3.950 m and Suni/Titicaca Altiplano basins up to 4.350 m) and explicit C1 Terra Preta anthropogenic intensity coupling on pre-contact horizons (strictly capped below 1.250 m with zero Andean bleed), the resulting kriged and population benchmark surfaces exhibit both 2,95× to 3,41× higher density in the Bolivian Highlands than in the Bolivian Lowlands and 3,73× to 6,15× higher pre-contact density across Amazonian Terra Preta corridors than across extra-Amazonian Eastern and Southern Brazil (inverting naturally after 1650AD to 0,87× by 1750AD as colonial coastal settlement overtook depopulated Amazonia).

To transform these discrete archaeological point observations into continuous demographic surfaces, PRETA aggregates sites onto 1.272 sliver-merged HydroBASINS Level 6 hydrological catchments (1.040 domestic catchments plus 232 cross-frontier Andean and South American conditioning catchments within a 400 km belt), achieving 99,90% domestic coverage (1.039 active domestic catchments). Spatial interpolation solves a two-scale non-stationary Matérn covariance model ($\nu = 3/2$) following Paciorek and Schervish (2006) [@PaciorekSchervish2006]:

$$C(x_i, x_j) = \sigma^2 \frac{2^{1-\nu}}{\Gamma(\nu)} |\Sigma_i|^{1/4} |\Sigma_j|^{1/4} \left| \frac{\Sigma_i + \Sigma_j}{2} \right|^{-1/2} (2\sqrt{\nu} Q_{ij})^\nu K_\nu(2\sqrt{\nu} Q_{ij})$$

where:

$$Q_{ij} = \sqrt{(x_i - x_j)^T \left( \frac{\Sigma_i + \Sigma_j}{2} \right)^{-1} (x_i - x_j)}$$

with $\nu = 3/2$, local riverine/valley clustering range $\tau_1 = 1,50$ (dimensionless) and regional dispersal range $\tau_2 = 2,78$ (dimensionless). Strict dasymetric habitability tapering achieves an uninhabited leakage ratio of 0,0001 and a logarithmic correlation of 0,8693 against HYDE 3.5 across 144.445 valid 5-arcminute terrestrial cells (Figure 2).

```{r fig2-kriging, results='asis'}
  "figures/fig2_preta_terra_preta_kriging.png",
  "Terra Preta anthrosol kriging and archaeological density surfaces across Amazonia.",
  "fig:kriging"
)
```

# Long-Run Demographic Trajectories (10000BC to 2026AD)

The demographic evolution of PRETA across twelve millennia reveals four major phases: pre-Columbian expansion, the post-contact epidemiological collapse, colonial divergence and modern national growth (Figure 3 and Table 3).

## Pre-Columbian Holocene Expansion (10000BC to 1500AD)

Human occupation of the PRETA domain began during the terminal Pleistocene, establishing an initial forager baseline of 60,95k in 10000BC (mean density 0,005 persons/km²). Early populations were concentrated in coastal environments and accessible river caves, notably the Caverna da Pedra Pintada near Monte Alegre, where foragers exploited forest fruits, river fish and freshwater molluscs [@Roosevelt1996]. Along the southern and south-eastern Atlantic coast, coastal fisher-hunter-gatherers constructed massive shell mounds (sambaquis) that served as permanent residential bases, territorial monuments and burial grounds from 6000BC onward.

Between 8000BC and 3000BC, Middle Holocene plant management and early cultivation lifted domain population to 226,3k. In the Llanos de Moxos, early inhabitants cultivated manioc and squash on artificial forest islands created in seasonally flooded savannas as early as 8000BC [@Lombardo2020]. The subsequent adoption of ceramic containers between 3000BC and 1000BC (Mina culture in Pará, Pocó traditions along the Trombetas) facilitated food storage and root detoxification, accelerating population growth to 718,5k in 1000BC.

During the Formative and Classic horizons (1000BC to 1000AD), the formation of fertile Terra Preta anthrosols allowed sedentary agricultural communities to establish dense, long-lasting settlements. Ceramic styles diversified into regional traditions, including the Barrancoid, Incised and Punctate, and Amazonian Polychrome traditions [@Neves2022]. Population rose to 2,05M at 1AD and 4,42M at 1000AD.

Between 1000AD and 1500AD, the domain reached its pre-Columbian zenith at 11,55M inhabitants (comprising 3,65M in the Peruvian-Ecuadorian Andean Sierra, 1,41M in the Bolivian Highlands and 6,49M across the lowland Amazonian, extra-Amazonian Brazilian and Guianese basins). Dense polities flourished across all six macro-regions:

1. In the Eastern Amazon (1,56M inhabitants at 1500AD), the Marajoara culture constructed dozens of monumental earthen mounds across Marajó Island, housing complex stratified chiefdoms [@Schaan2008]. Along the lower Amazon, the Tapajó chiefdom established a major urban centre at Santarém, with continuous settlements extending along river bluffs and interior plateaus [@Nimuendaju1952]. In the Upper Xingu, Kuikuro ancestors developed integrated networks of walled garden towns linked by formal roads and causeways, sustaining 30k to 50k people in an engineered parkland [@Heckenberger2003].
2. In the Western Amazon and Peruvian-Ecuadorian Andean Headwaters (6,24M inhabitants at 1500AD), the Peruvian-Ecuadorian Andean Sierra (3,65M) anchored the imperial urbanism of Cusco, Wari, Hatun Xauxa, Huánuco Pampa, Cajamarca, Chachapoyas and Tomebamba [@Cook1981; @Bauer2004; @DAltroy2015], while six lowland divisions (2,59M) housed the Casarabe stepped pyramids of Llanos de Moxos, Acre geoglyphs, Central Amazon Terra Preta bluffs and Upano Valley garden cities [@Prumers2022; @Peripato2023; @deSouza2018; @Rostain2024].
3. In the Bolivian Highlands (1,41M inhabitants at 1500AD), Lake Titicaca raised-field agriculture, Tiwanaku's urban legacy (35k peak at 800–1000AD), Aymara *señorío* pastoralism and Inca *Qullasuyu* maize estates in Cochabamba, Chuquiabo-La Paz and Charcas sustained highland densities an order of magnitude above the surrounding Amazonian lowlands [@Stanish2003; @Janusek2008; @Capriles2023].
4. In Southern Brazil (1,20M inhabitants at 1500AD), Southern Jê communities constructed semi-subterranean pit-house settlements and ceremonial enclosure mounds across the Araucaria highlands, while Guarani agriculturalists occupied the fertile terraces of the Paraná and Uruguay valleys.
5. In North-Eastern Brazil (940k inhabitants at 1500AD), Tupinambá horticulturalists occupied large palisaded villages along the Atlantic coast, while nomadic Macro-Jê groups occupied the interior Caatinga and São Francisco corridor.
6. In the Guianas (204k inhabitants at 1500AD), indigenous farmers constructed thousands of raised agricultural fields along the coastal savannahs to manage seasonal flooding, while inland polities built ditch-enclosed hill settlements [@Rostain2008].

## Columbian Epidemiological Collapse (1500AD to 1750AD)

The arrival of Europeans initiated a profound demographic catastrophe. Old World pathogens—smallpox, measles, influenza, typhus and yellow fever—spread through native trade networks, often travelling far ahead of physical contact with Europeans [@Newson1995; @Hemming1978]. Francisco de Orellana's 1542AD expedition down the Amazon reported continuous settlements extending for leagues along riverbanks. When Portuguese and Spanish expeditions revisited these sections in the seventeenth century, many formerly populous riverfronts were deserted, their inhabitants having succumbed to epidemics or fled into remote interfluvial forests [@Sweet1974].

The spatial heterogeneity of the demographic collapse was strongly modulated by hydrology and settlement morphology. Highly nucleated, linear settlements along the várzea floodplains of the Amazon, Tapajós and Solimões mainstems experienced immediate, catastrophic mortality due to high population densities, continuous riverine communication corridors and direct exposure to European exploratory fleets and indigenous slaving parties. In contrast, dispersed populations inhabiting the interfluvial terra firme forests and headwater tributaries were shielded by physical distance and environmental friction. Many várzea survivors fled inland into remote interfluvial zones, adopting mobile foraging strategies and low-visibility settlement layouts that masked their presence from colonial observers. Consequently, while riverine chiefdoms disintegrated within two generations of initial contact, interfluvial groups retained cultural and demographic continuity, albeit at substantially lower aggregate densities.

Along the Brazilian coast, Portuguese sugar plantations relied initially on enslaving coastal Tupinambá and Tupiniquim populations. Repeated epidemics in the 1550s and 1560s decimated coastal villages, prompting the Portuguese to organise inland slaving expeditions (*bandeiras*) that penetrated deep into the interior, capturing hundreds of thousands of indigenous captives and destabilising native demographic structures across the Paraná and Paraguay basins [@Hemming1978; @Marcilio1984]. Brazil's aggregate population collapsed from 4,00M in 1500AD to a nadir of 1,97M in 1600AD (a 51% decline overall, with indigenous losses exceeding 80%).

In the Spanish Amazon, missionary reductions established by the Jesuits in Maynas and Moxos and by Franciscans in Quijos and Caquetá suffered recurrent epidemic mortality [@Block1994; @Newson1995]. The Spanish Amazon population declined from 1,325M in 1542AD to a nadir of 467k in 1780AD (a 65% drop). In Paraguay, the concentration of Guaraní into encomiendas and thirty Jesuit missions provided partial protection from bandeirante raids, but mission populations suffered severe mortality during smallpox epidemics in the 1630s and 1730s, reaching an initial trough of 158k in 1620AD before stabilising around 193k by 1811AD [@Maeder1980; @Alden1996].

## Colonial Divergence and Forced Migration (1650AD to 1825AD)

From the late seventeenth century onward, regional demographic trajectories diverged sharply based on economic orientation:

1. In Brazil, the exhaustion of indigenous coastal labour led to massive transatlantic forced migration from West and Central Africa. Between 1550AD and the cessation of the slave trade in 1850AD, over 4,8M enslaved Africans arrived in Brazil, transforming the demographic and cultural fabric of Bahia, Pernambuco and Rio de Janeiro [@Curtin1969; @Klein2010; @Schwartz1985]. The discovery of gold in Minas Gerais in the 1690s triggered the first major interior gold rush in the Americas, attracting over 600k Portuguese immigrants and shifting Brazil's economic centre of gravity to the south-central highlands [@Alden1963; @Marcilio1984]. By 1800AD, Brazil's population had recovered to 3,48M, reaching 4,54M at independence in 1822AD.
2. In the Guianas, Dutch, British and French colonial authorities developed export plantation enclaves along the coastal estuaries, importing over 300k enslaved Africans to clear coastal mangrove swamps and build polder systems [@Oostindie2005]. High mortality and low fertility on sugar estates required continuous slave imports. Simultaneously, groups of enslaved Africans escaped into the interior rainforests, establishing autonomous Maroon communities (Ndyuka, Saramaka, Aluku) that maintained independent demographic growth.
3. In Paraguay, a unique mestizo society developed around Asunción. Because few Spanish women migrated to the province, intermarriage with Guaraní women became ubiquitous, creating a bilingual, culturally distinct population. The thirty Jesuit Guaraní missions maintained an average population of 100k to 140k until the expulsion of the Jesuits in 1767AD, after which secular administration led to the dispersion of mission residents into surrounding agrarian districts [@Maeder1980; @Alden1996].

## Modern National Expansion (1811AD to 2026AD)

The nineteenth and twentieth centuries brought unprecedented population growth across the domain:

1. Brazil expanded from 4,25M in 1822AD to 10,00M in the first official national census of 1872 [@IBGE1874]. The expansion of the São Paulo coffee economy attracted over 4,5M European immigrants (predominantly Italian, Portuguese, Spanish and German) and Japanese settlers between 1880AD and 1930AD. Rapid industrialisation, falling infant mortality and sustained fertility lifted Brazil's population to 41,24M in 1940, 119,00M in 1980, 203,08M in the 2022 census and 212,58M (~213M) by 2026AD [@IBGE2023]. The opening of the Transamazonian Highway and the expansion of cattle ranching and soy agriculture transformed the Amazonian interior, where regional population grew from less than 2,0M in 1950 to over 28M in 2026AD.
2. Bolivia grew from 1,18M at independence in 1825AD to 1,45M in 1846, 2,70M in 1950 and 11,53M in 2026AD [@INE_Bolivia_2024]. A transformative internal migration shifted the demographic balance from the historic mining centres of Potosí and the Altiplano to the eastern department of Santa Cruz, which expanded from a modest provincial town into the nation's largest metropolis.
3. Paraguay experienced the most catastrophic military shock in modern South American history during the War of the Triple Alliance (1864-1870AD). Allied armies from Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay subjected Paraguay to total warfare. Famine, cholera and battlefield casualties reduced Paraguay's population from 489k in 1864AD to 221k in 1870AD, eliminating an estimated 55% of the total population and up to 80% of adult males [@WhighamPotthast1999; @Whigham2002; @Maeder1984]. Post-war recovery was slow but accelerated in the twentieth century through high natural fertility and agricultural colonisation, reaching 6,28M by 2026AD [@INE_Paraguay_2022].
4. The Three Guianas followed distinct post-emancipation paths. In British Guiana and Dutch Suriname, plantation owners recruited over 400k indentured labourers from British India, Java and China between 1838AD and 1917AD, creating plural societies with distinct ethnic divisions [@BOS_Guyana_2016; @ABS_Suriname_2014]. French Guiana remained sparsely populated, functioning as a penal colony between 1852AD and 1953AD, before being revitalised by the construction of the Guiana Space Centre at Kourou in the 1960s [@INSEE_Guyane_2023]. By 2026AD, the Three Guianas hold 1,73M residents (Guyana 815k, Suriname 623k, French Guiana 288k).

Evaluating PRETA against established global baselines highlights substantial differences in pre-modern population numbers and spatial distributions (Table 3).

The divergences between PRETA and global compilations stem from three primary methodological differences:

## Pre-Columbian Underestimation in Twentieth-Century Syntheses

In pre-Columbian totals, McEvedy and Jones (1978) estimated 1,75M across the lowland PRETA domain in 1500AD, assigning 1,0M to Brazil and 750k to the remaining tropical territories [@McEvedyJones1978]. This minimalist total reflected mid-twentieth-century environmental determinism, which presumed that tropical soils could not sustain dense sedentary populations. Angus Maddison adopted similarly conservative figures, failing to account for indigenous agricultural terraforming [@Maddison2001]. HYDE 3.2 improved upon this by incorporating broader regional literature, but its domain total of 3,52M in 1500AD still significantly underestimates population in areas with documented earthwork and raised-field infrastructure [@KleinGoldewijk2017]. PRETA's bottom-up reconstruction indicates 6,49M inhabitants across lowland Amazonia, Brazil and the Guianas in 1500AD—aligning closely with William Denevan's regional estimate of 5,6M to 6,8M [@Denevan1992]—plus 5,06M across the Peruvian-Ecuadorian Andean Sierra (3,65M) and Bolivian Highlands (1,41M) for an integrated domain total of 11,55M.

A major factor behind twentieth-century undercounting was the reliance on shifting cultivation models that assumed regional carrying capacity could not exceed 0,2 to 0,5 persons/km² across tropical lowland soils [@Meggers1957]. Modern historical demography and geoarchaeology have demonstrated that indigenous populations overcame soil nutrient limitations through intensive polycultural agroforestry, raised-field wetland cultivation and dark-earth anthrosol engineering [@Denevan1992; @LiviBacci2007; @Clement2015]. In nucleated settlements such as Santarém, the Upper Xingu plaza villages and the Casarabe urban complexes in Moxos, localized population densities reached 10 to 30 persons/km², supported by perennial tree crops, riverine fisheries and enriched anthrosols that sustained continuous multi-cropping across generations [@Heckenberger2003; @Prumers2022; @Glaser2004].

## Gridded Allocation Biases in Global Earth System Models

The spatial distribution of population differs fundamentally between top-down global databases and PRETA. In HYDE 3.1 and HYDE 3.2, downscaling algorithms rely heavily on distance to major navigable rivers and universal elevation penalties [@KleinGoldewijk2010; @KleinGoldewijk2017]. In contrast, PRETA's non-stationary Matérn kriging, informed by 64.713 deduplicated archaeological records (including 17.022 Peru SIGDA monuments and Qhapaq Ñan nodes, 5.542 Colombia ICANH sites, 4.693 p3k14c/AndesC14 dates, 2.197 XRONOS Bolivia-Peru dates, 316 Bolivian Highlands survey hubs and 1.323 Terra Preta contexts) and calibrated to both the tropical Andean vertical archipelago and pre-contact Terra Preta anthropogenic intensity, simultaneously captures the Central Andean and Bolivian Highland agrarian heartlands (Cusco, Wari, Tiwanaku, Lake Titicaca, La Paz, Oruro, Cochabamba, Potosí, Cajamarca and Chachapoyas — with Bolivian Highlands 2,95× to 3,41× denser than Bolivian Lowlands) alongside dense interfluvial lowland settlements across the Upper Xingu, Acre, Llanos de Moxos and Santarém (with Terra Preta Amazonia 3,73× to 6,15× denser than extra-Amazonian Eastern and Southern Brazil pre-contact) [@SIGDA2024; @ICANH2024; @Capriles2023; @Heckenberger2003; @Peripato2023; @Prumers2022; @Stenborg2012].

Global Earth system models also apply continuous spatial smoothing that obscures sharp hydrological and geomorphological boundaries. In contrast, PRETA constrains demographic allocation within 1.272 sliver-merged HydroBASINS Level 6 drainage catchments, preventing demographic leakage across continental divides and eliminating small-polygon areal singularities. By coupling dasymetric habitability tapers with local covariance tensors ($\tau_1 = 1,50$, $\tau_2 = 2,78$), PRETA captures both the terraced imperial highlands of Peru and Bolivia and the dual riverine-anthrosol structure of lowland Amazonia.

## Asynchronous Regional Collapse and Modern Convergence

The timing and depth of the post-contact demographic collapse are captured with greater historical fidelity in PRETA. Global models typically impose a uniform continent-wide trough at 1600AD or 1650AD. In reality, the collapse was asynchronous across river basins. On the Brazilian coast, intensive contact and slaving drove the population to a nadir at 1600AD (1,97M). In Paraguay, mission concentration and epidemic cycles delayed the trough to 1620AD (158k). In the upper Amazon and Moxos missions, where direct Spanish presence was established later, epidemic depopulation continued through the eighteenth century, reaching a nadir in 1780AD (467k).

This temporal divergence reflects differing colonial economic structures and epidemic diffusion corridors. In Portuguese Brazil, the rapid expansion of the sugar plantation economy along the Atlantic coast created an insatiable demand for forced labour that depleted indigenous coastal populations within decades, necessitating the early importation of enslaved Africans [@Marcilio1984; @Schwartz1985]. In contrast, in the Spanish Amazon and Paraguay, Jesuit and Franciscan missionary networks congregated indigenous populations into compact reductions that acted as epidemiological cauldrons during outbreaks, but simultaneously provided institutional protection against external slaving raids [@Block1994; @Maeder1980].

By the late nineteenth century, as modern statistical censuses were instituted across the independent nations (Brazil's 1872 census, Bolivia's 1846 count and post-Triple Alliance Paraguayan surveys), PRETA and global baselines converge, with discrepancies dropping below 3% in modern census horizons [@IBGE1874; @IBGE2023].

# Limitations and Future Directions

While PRETA provides a bottom-up reconstruction of South American historical population, several methodological and evidentiary limitations remain:

First, the distribution of catalogued archaeological sites in national registers, particularly IPHAN SICG, is subject to geographical survey bias. Archaeological impact assessments in Brazil are concentrated along infrastructure corridors, hydroelectric reservoirs, mining concessions and expanding agricultural frontiers in Pará, Mato Grosso and Rondônia. In contrast, large sections of the central and northern Amazon rainforest, including the Rio Negro and Japurá interfluves, remain archaeologically under-surveyed. As airborne LiDAR surveys expand across primary forest, additional pre-Columbian earthwork complexes will likely be identified, requiring periodic recalibration of regional covariance parameters [@Peripato2023].

Second, radiocarbon taphonomy in humid tropical environments presents inherent preservation challenges. High soil acidity, warm temperatures and abundant moisture accelerate the microbial degradation of organic materials, bones and plant remains. Consequently, early Holocene rockshelter and coastal shell-mound contexts are over-represented relative to open-air tropical forest forager sites, potentially leading to conservative estimates for early pre-ceramic horizons [@Roosevelt1996; @Lombardo2020].

Third, colonial ecclesiastical and administrative registers systematically omitted uncontacted indigenous groups (*indios bravos*) and autonomous Maroon communities (*quilombos*) that actively avoided colonial control. While PRETA incorporates ethnohistorical estimates for non-reduced populations, these groups remain difficult to quantify with precision [@Hemming1978; @Sweet1974].

Fourth, historical census enumerations in early post-independence decades varied in territorial coverage and methodology. In Paraguay, the pre-war population in 1864AD has been subject to extensive demographic debate, with estimates ranging from 350k to 525k; PRETA's baseline of 489k is anchored to Whigham and Potthast's critical re-analysis of the 1846 and 1864 parish returns [@WhighamPotthast1999; @Whigham2002; @Maeder1984]. In Bolivia, nineteenth-century enumerations under-counted non-tributary lowland indigenous populations in the Oriente, requiring adjustments based on Franciscan mission registers [@INE_Bolivia_2024; @Block1994].

Fifth, boundary adjustments across successive administrative regimes complicate longitudinal micro-data linkage. In Brazil, the number of second-level administrative divisions (municípios) expanded from fewer than 1.500 at the time of the 1872 census to 5.570 in 2026AD, requiring dasymetric downscaling of early municipal aggregates onto contemporary geographic polygons.

Sixth, the spatial resolution of early colonial cartography involves toponymic shifting. Indigenous groups frequently relocated settlements following epidemic outbreaks or punitive slaving expeditions, meaning that historical village names documented in sixteenth-century chronicles do not always correspond to fixed geographical coordinates.

Future iterations of PRETA will benefit from three developing methodologies: airborne LiDAR coverage across unlogged primary forests, environmental DNA (eDNA) from lake-sediment cores to reconstruct pre-Columbian crop cultivation and forest composition, and high-precision Bayesian radiocarbon chronologies to resolve micro-regional demographic shifts. Sedimentary eDNA offers the prospect of directly detecting ancient crop cultivation (such as manioc, maize and sweet potato) and forest canopy composition independent of macroscopic charcoal preservation, identifying pre-Columbian agrarian occupations in areas where acid oxisols have degraded macro-botanical remains.

Seventh, radiocarbon dates as demographic proxies require rigorous calibration against taphonomic decay curves. Summed probability distributions of radiocarbon dates can be biased by non-linear preservation loss in tropical environments, where older charcoal deposits are progressively fragmented by bioturbation, weathering and soil leaching. Future Bayesian modelling within PRETA will incorporate explicit taphonomic correction functions, linking archaeological radiocarbon sample frequencies directly to geomorphological sediment accumulation rates and pollen-stratigraphic agricultural markers.

Finally, historical cartographic toponymy and indigenous oral geographies provide critical opportunities for spatial ground-truthing. Ancient trans-continental trail systems, such as the pre-Columbian Peabiru routes linking the Atlantic coast of Santa Catarina and São Paulo to the Andean Altiplano, guided colonial exploration and subsequent highway networks. Reconstructing these ancestral corridors through high-resolution digital elevation models and satellite radar will clarify the diffusion paths of ceramic technologies, cultivated domesticates and post-Columbian epidemic pathogens across the South American interior.

By bridging archaeological point registers, colonial documentary archives and modern municipal census databases into a continuous, hydrologically nested spatial model, PRETA provides a grounded foundation for analysing long-run anthropogenic transformation across South America. Understanding the scale and spatial patterning of historical population is fundamental to determining pre-industrial forest modification, carbon-cycle dynamics and biodiversity baselines across the Amazon basin and adjacent biomes.
